references.title: Comparative efficacy and acceptability of 21 antidepressant drugs for the acute treatment of adults with major depressive disorder: a systematic review and network meta-analysis.
references.abstractSummary: Across 522 trials and 116,477 adults with acute major depressive disorder, every studied antidepressant outperformed placebo, while differences among active drugs were generally smaller and acceptability varied. The trials largely excluded treatment-resistant, psychotic, bipolar, and serious-medical-comorbidity populations, and certainty ranged from moderate to very low.

references.title: A network meta-analysis of the effects of psychotherapies, pharmacotherapies and their combination in the treatment of adult depression.
publicationTypes: Network meta-analysis verified from title and abstract
references.abstractSummary: Across 101 studies with 11,910 adults, combined psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy produced more response and remission than either alone; psychotherapy and pharmacotherapy alone did not differ materially. Most participants had moderate-to-severe depression, and evidence about long-term outcomes, particular treatments, and specific populations remained limited.

references.title: Psychotherapies for depression: a network meta-analysis covering efficacy, acceptability and long-term outcomes of all main treatment types.
publicationTypes: Network meta-analysis verified from title and abstract
references.abstractSummary: A network of 331 randomized trials with 34,285 patients found that the major psychotherapy families were effective and acceptable for acute adult depression, with few consistent differences among them. The analysis cannot establish patient-specific matching, and the authors emphasized preference and availability when choosing among broadly effective options.

references.title: Risk factors for suicidal thoughts and behaviors: A meta-analysis of 50 years of research.
references.abstractSummary: Across 365 longitudinal studies, isolated risk factors predicted suicidal outcomes only slightly better than chance, and performance did not improve over five decades. This supports caution about single-factor prediction but does not determine an individual patient's disposition or substitute for a structured safety assessment.

references.title: Combining Antidepressants vs Antidepressant Monotherapy for Treatment of Patients With Acute Depression: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis.
references.abstractSummary: Thirty-nine randomized trials with 6,751 patients found a modest average advantage for antidepressant combinations, particularly a reuptake inhibitor paired with a presynaptic alpha-2 antagonist; bupropion combinations were not superior to monotherapy. Heterogeneity and publication bias limit translation into a blanket rule for starting any two agents together.

references.title: Is electroconvulsive therapy an evidence-based treatment for catatonia? A systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.abstractSummary: Twenty-eight studies with 564 patients generally described catatonia improvement after ECT, but the randomized evidence could not be pooled and protocols varied. The authors concluded that the literature did not robustly establish efficacy or effectiveness, so this is context rather than a stand-alone gameplay rule.

references.title: Discontinuation of antidepressants after remission with antidepressant medication in major depressive disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
references.abstractSummary: Across 40 enrichment-design studies with 8,890 participants who had remitted on medication, continuing the same antidepressant was associated with substantially less relapse than switching to placebo. Patient-level relapse modifiers were sparsely studied, and the design does not answer every discontinuation or long-term maintenance question.
